title: The paste meant for a king
hookLine: Kubja gives Krishna the sandal paste she carried for a king, and is made straight; why home puja serves God with your own hands
carry: puja is serving god with your own hands
last: NAIVEDYA — WHEN GOD IS FED, EVERYONE IS FED.

cards: Krishna is a teenager, walking into the city of Mathura for the first time, the city of the cruel king Kamsa. On the street he meets a young woman bent nearly double, her back badly curved.
People call her Kubja, the hunchback. She's carrying a dish of fragrant sandalwood paste, the best in the city, for the king himself. Krishna smiles and asks: who's that for?
Could we have some? She looks up at him. It's the king's paste, and she is the king's servant.
She gives it anyway, generously, with her own hands, to Krishna and his brother.

teach.b: Krishna is delighted. He steps on her toes gently, puts two fingers under her chin, and lifts, and her back straightens. She stands tall for the first time in her life.
That's how the Bhagavata Purana tells it. Look at what she did. She served God with what was in her hands, the most precious thing she had.
Its offerings are called upacharas, services, the way you'd serve an honored guest.

teach.h: BELL, LAMP, FLOWER, WATER, SWEET, BOW.
teach.b: Old manuals give a short five-part form: fragrance, flower, incense, lamp and food. Fragrance comes first, often sandal paste, Kubja's gift, touched to the image.
This week you've learned the rest, and on a school morning it can all fit in four minutes. Ring the bell: you're calling God in. Light the lamp.
Offer a fresh flower, which stands for your heart. A few drops of water. Some sandal paste or incense if you have it.
Something sweet, which comes back as prasad. Then a name or a mantra said quietly, and pranam, the bow. Families do it in different orders, and some mornings it's only a lamp and a bow.
That counts too. Notice that nobody does it for you. No priest is needed at a home shrine.
Your own hands do the serving, the way Kubja's did. And many teachers read her straightened back simply: whoever serves God isn't left the same.

how: Many Hindu households do a short daily puja at the home shrine in the morning, serving the deity with their own hands: ringing a bell, lighting a lamp, offering sandal paste or incense, flowers, water and food, saying a mantra or a deity's name, bowing, and sharing the offered food as prasad. No priest is needed at home.

o: a long temple ceremony only a priest can lead
a short home worship done before the day begins
a blessing said over the first meal of the day

games.q: kubja's gift, your shelf — tap the pairs.
p: gave Krishna the paste meant for the king
fragrance, the first of the five offerings
a service offered to God, as to a guest
the bow that closes the welcome

s: puja at home can only be done by a priest
at home, families serve God with their own hands. no priest is needed.
Kubja gave Krishna the sandal paste she was carrying for the king
and Krishna lifted her chin and straightened her back.
some mornings it's only a lamp and a bow, and that is still service.

games.q: it's a rushed morning. you have one minute, not four. what fits today's teaching?
o: skip it: a half puja doesn't count.
light the lamp and bow: your hands still serve.
ask someone else to do it for you.
games.why: puja is service, not a checklist. a lamp lit and a bow, done with your own hands, still serves.

practice: However small your corner is, even if it's only in your mind, go through it once with your own hands. Ring a bell or tap a glass. Light the lamp, or picture it.

Set down a flower or a leaf, a few drops of water and a small piece of something sweet. If you pray, quietly say your mantra or a name you honor a few times. Then put your hands together, bow, and sit for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Morning puja. The home shrine, put together: bell, lamp, flower, water, sweet, a name and a bow, served with your own hands before the day begins.

orig.note: Sanskrit pūjā: honoring, worship. Your word from day eight.

carryVoice: Your line: puja is serving God with your own hands. Kubja gave what she carried. Day one hundred seventeen, and that's the week.
